fatal_errors: The proposed intervention is bulk grain refinement by severe plastic deformation, whereas the target intervention is an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating followed by annealing, especially at 550 °C.
The proposed molten-chloride conditions do not reproduce the target sulfuric-acid electrochemistry or 900 °C Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 hot-corrosion exposures.
explanation: This is a coherent and testable alternative hypothesis for chromium-bearing stainless steels, but it is not a reconstruction of the target study. It shares two mechanistic elements with the target—grain refinement and formation of a Cr-rich passive layer—and predicts compatible electrochemical trends such as lower Icorr and less pitting. However, it omits the AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating, atmospheric plasma spraying, the 550 °C annealing optimum, BCC/FCC phase behavior, Al-rich oxides, coating porosity and crack penetration, hardness changes, and cyclic hot-corrosion weight gain. The composition-matched coarse-grained control and combined electrochemical, XPS, and microscopy measurements provide a reasonably discriminating study, although SPD can alter residual stress, defect density, texture, and phase constitution in addition to grain size, so grain-boundary density is not fully isolated. Evidence E2 directly supports improved passivation and Cr enrichment in UFG stainless steels. E1 does not support the claimed molten-salt passivation benefit; it instead notes that Cr can be preferentially attacked in nuclear molten-salt environments. Thus, extrapolation from aqueous passivation to chloride or other molten salts is insufficiently supported. The falsification rule is useful but overly conjunctive: failure of either the corrosion improvement or Cr enrichment should challenge the proposed causal chain, rather than requiring both to fail.
